analysis.one_liner: Requires insurers to spend at least 90 cents of every premium dollar on medical care, with rebates for the shortfall.
analysis.headline: The bill, with only one cosponsor, was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any action before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar health insurers from selling any plan unless at least 90% of premium dollars went to actual medical care — the 'medical loss ratio' — with the rest limited to administration and profit. Insurers that fell short would have to rebate money back to their customers. The Secretary of Health and Human Services would define how the ratio is calculated, collect data from insurers, and enforce the rule with penalties. A version of this idea later became part of the 2010 health care law, but at lower percentages.
analysis.who_benefits: People who pay health insurance premiums. If an insurer spends more than 10% of premiums on overhead, marketing, and profit, it would have to send the difference back to enrollees as a rebate. The bill would also force insurers to report standardized data to HHS, making it easier to see how much of every premium actually pays for care.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a health insurance issuer from offering coverage unless it demonstrates a medical loss ratio of at least 90%, limiting how much of each premium can go to administration and profit.
Requires issuers to pay rebates to enrollees for any plan year in which coverage falls below the 90% ratio, so money that would have gone to overhead returns to customers.
Requires HHS to establish a uniform definition and calculation methodology for the medical loss ratio, and directs insurers to submit data starting in plan year 2011 so compliance can be verified.
Directs the Secretary to promulgate regulations for enforcing the requirement and to provide for appropriate penalties.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, which would lose the freedom to spend premium dollars on administrative costs, marketing, and profit beyond 10% of premiums, and would bear the cost of data reporting and any rebates owed.

drawbacks.text: A single 90% floor applies to all health insurance coverage, without any carve-out in the bill itself for small or individual-market plans; the Secretary could 'take into account the circumstances of different plans,' but the bill leaves that entirely to regulation rather than writing protections into law.
The whole rule depends on HHS defining the medical loss ratio and enforcement penalties, so its real strength would rest on future regulatory choices rather than the statute itself.
Rebates go to enrollees only when a plan falls below the floor; the bill does nothing about premium levels directly, so insurers could respond by raising prices rather than shrinking overhead.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is straightforward and meaningful: it would shift premium dollars from overhead and profit back to patients through mandatory rebates. The main design weaknesses are that the 90% floor is uniform while the flexibility for different plan types is left to regulators, and that enforcement is delegated to HHS rulemaking — so the bill's value would depend heavily on how the Secretary wrote the rules.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the bill on September 30, 2009, with Rep. John Tierney as the only cosponsor.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction, and the next day to the Subcommittee on Health.
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a committee vote, a hearing-based markup, or a floor vote, and it died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers were better off, since they kept for a few more months the freedom to spend premium dollars on administration and profit without a 90% floor and rebate obligation. Congress did ultimately adopt a medical loss ratio requirement in the 2010 health care law, but at lower thresholds — 80–85% rather than the 90% this bill demanded — so the stricter standard never took effect.

for.name: Rep. Keith Ellison
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited its single cosponsor; no committee or floor action followed.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 30, 2009, and never reported the bill out; the last action in the record is the referral to its Health subcommittee the following day.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Health
against.role: Subcommittee of referral, Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on October 1, 2009, and took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Democratic sponsorship — one sponsor and one cosponsor among 253 House Democrats — and no Republicans signed on; the record shows no votes, so partisan support cannot be measured beyond cosponsorship.

industries.note: The bill would cap what insurers can keep for administration, marketing, and profit at 10% of premiums and force rebates when they fall short, directly reducing the portion of premiums they control. Insurers' interest in keeping that share ran against premium payers who would receive the rebates.
